q.intro.text: Ridgeview Middle has two hundred seventh graders. The student council wants their mean homework time last night.

q.draw.text: Maya draws ten names from a hat: their mean is forty-six minutes. Leo puts the names back and draws ten: thirty-four minutes.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the board.

e.s1.text: The population is all two hundred seventh graders: everyone the question is about. The sample is the ten names Maya drew, by chance.

e.s2.text: Maya’s ten times add up to four hundred sixty minutes. Four hundred sixty divided by ten is forty-six: the sample mean, our estimate for all two hundred.

e.s3.text: Draw again, and again: twenty random samples of ten. Each dot is one sample’s mean. They run from thirty-four to fifty and a half.

e.s4.text: The planner app logged everyone: the mean of all two hundred is forty-two. Most sample means land within six minutes of it.

e.why.text: Quick check: why don’t the twenty sample means all equal forty-two?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Chance picks a different ten each time, so each mean comes out a little different. That is sampling variability, not a mistake.

e.w-mirror.text: Every one of these samples was drawn fairly. A fair random sample lands near the population mean, not on it.

e.w-dot.text: Look at the bottom plot again: each dot is the mean of a whole sample of ten, not one student.

t.intro.text: Now each sample has forty students. Step one is done for you.

t.mean.text: This sample’s forty times add up to one thousand seven hundred twenty minutes. What is the sample mean?

t.m-ok.text: Yes: one thousand seven hundred twenty divided by forty is forty-three. Our estimate: about forty-three minutes for all two hundred.

t.m-ten.text: There are forty students in this sample, not ten. Divide by forty.

t.m-other.text: Share the total equally: one thousand seven hundred twenty divided by forty.

t.predict.text: Predict: twenty random samples of forty. Compared with the means of samples of ten, their means will be…

t.p-ok.text: Right. A mean of forty times averages out more highs and lows, so the means bunch closer.

t.p-same.text: The students vary as much as ever, in the top plot. But a mean of forty averages out more highs and lows: watch the bottom plot.

t.p-more.text: More students in a sample make its mean steadier, not wilder. Watch the bottom plot.

t.far.text: Most of the twenty means of forty land within about how far of forty-two?

t.f-ok.text: Yes: within about three minutes, half as far as with samples of ten.

t.f-six.text: Six minutes was for samples of ten. Look at the bottom plot: the means of forty bunch tighter.

t.f-14.text: Fourteen minutes is how far single students typically are from forty-two. Means of forty vary far less.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you said both samples were fair estimates, and you were right: random samples vary. Now you can see how much, and that bigger samples vary less.

t.cb-mirror.text: At the start you thought one of them made a mistake. Now you have seen twenty fair samples: none of them matched exactly. Random samples vary.

t.cb-exact.text: At the start you picked exactly forty. The mean of all two hundred is forty-two: two samples give estimates, never the exact value.

t.cb-none.text: At the start: Maya’s forty-six and Leo’s thirty-four are both fair estimates. Random samples vary, and bigger samples vary less.

p.intro.text: Ridgeview also ran an online poll: sixty seventh graders chose to answer, mean fifty-five minutes. Jordan says: sixty answers beat forty, so fifty-five is the better estimate. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: A random sample of forty lands near the mean of all two hundred, give or take chance, because every student had the same chance to be picked.

p.c2.text: the poll’s sixty lean toward students with lots of homework, because students with a lot of homework are the most likely to answer a poll about it.

p.c3.text: so the poll misses the same way every time, however many answer, because more answers shrink chance error, not the error from how the sample was chosen.

p.x-big.text: More volunteers lean the same way. Size shrinks chance error, not a lean in who answers.

p.x-honest.text: Everyone can answer honestly and the poll still misses: the problem is who answered, not lying.

p.x-mirror.text: A random sample lands near the population mean, not exactly on it. That is not the reason here.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That’s the proof. Random samples miss by chance, both ways, and less when they are bigger. The poll misses by thirteen minutes, the same way every time: that is bias, and more answers don’t fix it.
